activities.title: Contour Hill: slice a clay hill with water

materials.item: modelling clay or plasticine
a clear plastic box with a clear lid, about 15 centimetres long and 8 centimetres deep
a cup of water and a spoon
a marker pen that wipes off
a ruler
a sheet of paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Build a clay hill, add water in 1 centimetre steps, and trace the water's edge on the lid each time.

activities.record: The paper with the rings you traced, labelled with the height of each ring, and a drawing of the steepest and gentlest sides.

flow.do: Shape a clay hill about 5 centimetres high, with a steep side and a gentle side. Press it firmly onto the floor of the box. Mark lines on the outside of the box at 1, 2, 3 and 4 centimetres above the floor.
flow.say: Make a hill. One side is steep. One side is gentle. Mark the box at 1, 2, 3 and 4 centimetres.
flow.kid: Make a clay hill. Mark the box wall at 1, 2, 3 and 4 centimetres.

ask.q: What do you think the rings will look like from above?
good: Far apart on the gentle side.

flow.parent: Do not say what the rings look like. Let your child guess. Press the clay down so the water cannot creep underneath.
flow.context: This is the first step of Contour Hill. You build a clay hill in a clear box and get ready to slice it with water.

flow.do: Pour water slowly into the box until it reaches the 1 centimetre line. Put the lid on. Look straight down at the lid. Trace the edge of the water on the hill with the marker. Take the lid off, pour more water to 2 centimetres, and trace again. Repeat for 3 and 4 centimetres.
flow.say: Add water to the first line. Look straight down and trace where the water meets the hill. Add more water. Trace again.
flow.kid: Add water to each line. Trace the water's edge on the lid.
flow.parent: Look straight down, or the line will be drawn in the wrong place. The rings are the contour lines of your hill. Each one joins places at the same height. The clay must stay firmly pressed or the water will creep underneath.

flow.do: Lay the lid on paper. Trace the rings with a pencil. Write the height beside each ring: 1, 2, 3 and 4 centimetres. Compare the rings on the steep side and the gentle side.
flow.say: Trace your rings on the paper. Write each height. Where are the rings close together? Where are they far apart?
flow.kid: Trace the rings. Write the heights. Compare the two sides.

check.q: The rings are packed close together on one side of the hill. What does this tell you?
options: The land is steep on that side
The land is flat on that side
The hill is hollow on that side
check.why: Contour lines join places of equal height. Where the land rises fast, you cross many heights in a short distance, so the lines are close together.

flow.context: In this step you turn the rings on the lid into a contour map.

activities.context: In this activity you build a clay hill and slice it with water, to see how contour lines show a hill on a flat map.

activities.title: Two Maps of India: borders and land

materials.item: an atlas, or a wall map of India, or a map of India on a phone
a notebook and a pencil
colour pencils

schedule.what: Compare a political map and a physical map of India, and find where the land is high and which way the rivers flow.

activities.record: A list of what each map shows that the other does not, and a sketch of India with the Western Ghats, the Deccan and the rivers marked.

flow.do: Find your state on a political map. Write the names of two states that share a border with it. Find your state on the physical map. What colour is it?
flow.say: Find our state on the political map. Which states touch it? Now find it on the physical map. What colour is it?
flow.kid: Find our state on both maps.
flow.context: This is a map reading activity. You compare a political map and a physical map of India.

flow.do: On the physical map, find the Western Ghats, the Deccan plateau and the Eastern Ghats. Find the Ganga plain. Say which areas are high and which are low.
flow.say: Where are the high lands on the map? What colour are they? Where is the lowest land?
flow.kid: Find the Western Ghats and the Deccan. Which is higher?

ask.q: What do the colours on the physical map tell you?

flow.parent: Most physical maps use green for low land and brown for high land. A key on the map says what each colour means.

flow.do: Find the sources and ends of the Kaveri, the Godavari and the Narmada. Which way does each flow? Which rivers flow to the east and which to the west?
flow.say: Where do these rivers begin and end? Which way does each one flow? What does that tell you about the slope of the land?
flow.kid: Follow three rivers. Which way does each flow?

check.q: Most of the large rivers of peninsular India, such as the Kaveri and the Godavari, flow east. What does this tell you about the land?
options: The land slopes down towards the east
The land slopes down towards the west
check.why: Rivers flow downhill. If they flow east towards the Bay of Bengal, the land tilts down to the east. The Western Ghats are high, so many rivers begin near them and flow east across the plateau. The Narmada flows west because it runs in a rift valley.

flow.context: In this step you follow rivers on the physical map to find which way the land slopes.

activities.context: In this activity you compare a political map and a physical map of India, and use the second to find where the land is high and which way the rivers flow.

activities.title: Map Mistakes: draw a map with five mistakes

materials.item: two sheets of squared paper
pencils and an eraser
a ruler
a grown-up or a friend to swap with

schedule.what: Each person draws a map of a room with five planted mistakes, then swaps and finds them.

activities.record: Your map with the mistakes circled, and a list of what each mistake would do to a reader.

flow.do: Draw a map of your room. Hide five mistakes in the map. Choose from these. Leave out the key. Leave out the north arrow. Draw the door on the wrong wall. Draw one wall too long. Use one symbol for two things.
flow.say: Draw a map of your room. Hide five mistakes in it, and do not tell me which. I will draw one too.
flow.kid: Draw a map with five hidden mistakes.
flow.parent: Draw your own as well, so the child searches for yours. A mistake should be something a reader could notice by checking the map against the room.
flow.context: This is a game-like activity. You draw a map on purpose with five mistakes, and a friend must find them.

flow.do: Swap maps. Walk round the room with the map you were given. Circle every mistake you find.
flow.say: Swap maps. Check each thing on the map against the room. Circle the mistakes.
flow.kid: Swap maps. Find the mistakes.

ask.q: Which mistake was the easiest to find, and which was the hardest?
good: A wall drawn too long was harder.
A wrong door was easy to check.

flow.parent: A good map can be checked. Walk the room with the map in your hand.

flow.do: Talk about the mistakes. Which would cause the most trouble for a visitor?
flow.say: Which mistake would send a visitor the wrong way? Which one only makes the map harder to read?
flow.kid: Which mistake is the worst for a visitor?

check.q: Which mistake would send a visitor to the wrong place?
options: The door drawn on the wrong wall
check.why: A door on the wrong wall puts something in the wrong place, which sends a visitor the wrong way. A missing key or title makes the map harder to read, but the places are still right.

flow.context: In this step you decide which mistakes matter most.

activities.context: In this activity you draw a map of your room with five hidden mistakes, and find the mistakes in a map drawn by someone else.

activities.title: Our Latitude and Longitude: where on Earth is home?

materials.item: a phone or tablet with a map app
a notebook and a pencil
a globe or an atlas, if you have one
a grown-up to handle the phone

schedule.what: Find the latitude and longitude of home, and compare with Chennai and Delhi.

activities.record: The latitude and longitude of your home, and a sentence comparing it with Delhi.

flow.do: Open the map app. Press and hold on your home until a pin appears. Read the two numbers at the top of the screen or in the pin's details. Write them down.
flow.say: Press and hold on our home. The phone shows two numbers. The first is the latitude. The second is the longitude. Write both.
flow.kid: Press and hold on home. Read the two numbers.
flow.parent: The two numbers are written in degrees, for example 13.08, 80.27. The first is the latitude, the number of degrees north of the equator, and the second is the longitude, east of Greenwich. Chennai is at about 13 north and 80 east.
flow.context: This is a short activity to find the latitude and longitude of home on a phone.

flow.do: Find Delhi, at about 28.6 north and 77.2 east. Is Delhi north or south of your home? How can you tell from the numbers? Find the equator on the globe or atlas.
flow.say: Delhi is at about 28.6 north. Is it north or south of us? How do the numbers tell you? How far north of the equator are we?
flow.kid: Is Delhi north or south of home? How do the numbers tell you?
flow.parent: One degree of latitude is about 111 kilometres, so the difference of about 15.6 degrees is around 1,700 kilometres.

check.q: Home is at 13 degrees north. Delhi is at 28.6 degrees north. Which is further north?
check.why: A bigger latitude number means further north of the equator. 28.6 is bigger than 13, so Delhi is further north.

flow.do: Talk. Why is a pair of numbers enough to name any place on Earth?
flow.say: Why does a place on Earth need two numbers? Could one number be enough?
flow.kid: Why does a place need two numbers?
flow.think: What if you only had the latitude? Where could you be?

activities.context: In this activity you use a phone to find the latitude and longitude of your home, and compare it with Delhi.

setup.caption: 1. Press and hold on home and read the two numbers.

projects.title: Zoom-Out Atlas: from your room to your city in five pages

materials.item: 5 sheets of paper of the same size
tracing paper or baking paper, enough for 3 pages
a ruler and a pencil
colour pencils
a phone or tablet with a map app, with a scale bar that shows at each zoom
a stapler or string to bind the pages
a grown-up to come on the walk

schedule.what: Page 1: draw your room, with 1 centimetre for 50 centimetres.
Page 2: draw the floor of your building, with 1 centimetre for 5 metres.
Page 3: walk the street, count steps, and draw it with 1 centimetre for 50 metres.
Page 4: trace the neighbourhood from the phone, with 1 centimetre for 500 metres.
Page 5: trace your city, with 1 centimetre for 5 kilometres.
Bind the pages and compare them.

projects.record: A five-page atlas, with a scale bar and a north arrow on each page, and a note on what appears and disappears as the scale shrinks.

flow.do: Page 1. Draw your room from above, using 1 centimetre for 50 centimetres. Measure the walls with a tape or count tiles. Draw the furniture. Draw a scale bar and a north arrow.
flow.say: Page 1 is your room. Each centimetre on the paper stands for 50 centimetres in the room. Draw the walls, the door and the bed.
flow.kid: Page 1: draw your room. 1 centimetre is 50 centimetres.

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the details when we make each page 10 times smaller?
good: The map will have more area but less detail.

flow.parent: A 4 metre by 3 metre room is 8 centimetres by 6 centimetres on the page. Each next page covers 10 times more distance, so the room becomes a dot by page 3.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Zoom-Out Atlas, a project in which you make five maps of your world, each one ten times smaller than the last.

flow.do: Page 2. Draw the whole floor of your building. Use 1 centimetre for 5 metres. Count your steps along the corridor and estimate the length of each flat. Show your room as a small box.
flow.say: Page 2 is your whole floor. Now 1 centimetre is 5 metres. Where is your room? It is smaller now.
flow.kid: Page 2: draw your floor. 1 centimetre is 5 metres.
flow.parent: A step is about half a metre, so ten steps is about 5 metres, which is 1 centimetre on the page.

flow.do: Page 3. Walk down your street with a grown-up. Count steps between landmarks. Draw the street with 1 centimetre for 50 metres. Put in the gate, the shop and a big tree.
flow.say: Page 3 is your street. 1 centimetre is 50 metres. About 100 steps make 1 centimetre. Where is your building now?
flow.kid: Page 3: draw the street. 1 centimetre is 50 metres.
flow.parent: Your room has disappeared, and the building is a small box. This is how a map shrinks the world.

flow.do: Page 4. On the phone, zoom out until the scale bar matches 500 metres. Lay tracing paper on the screen and trace the main roads, your home and three landmarks. Copy it onto your page.
flow.say: Page 4 is your neighbourhood. 1 centimetre is 500 metres. Trace the big roads. Many small streets will be gone.
flow.kid: Page 4: trace the neighbourhood from the phone.
flow.parent: Check the scale bar on the screen with a ruler. The scale changes if you zoom in or out, so measure it again.
flow.wait: Keep the pages. Come back on the day after tomorrow.

flow.do: Page 5. Zoom out again until the bar matches 5 kilometres. Trace the main roads, a river or a railway, and your home. Copy it onto your page.
flow.say: Page 5 is your city. 1 centimetre is 5 kilometres. Is your home still on the map? What does it look like now?
flow.kid: Page 5: trace your city. 1 centimetre is 5 kilometres.

check.q: On which page does a single house take up the most space?
check.why: Page 1 has the largest scale, so it shows things biggest. By page 5, a house is a tiny dot or has vanished altogether.

flow.context: In this step you draw the last page of the atlas, the whole city.

flow.do: Put the five pages in order and bind them. Compare them. What stays on every page, and what disappears? Write three sentences.
flow.say: Look at all five pages. What is on every page? What disappears as the scale shrinks? Why?
flow.kid: Compare the pages. What disappears? Why?

ask.q: What is on every page, and what disappears?
good: Big roads stay on every page.
Small things vanish when the scale gets small.

flow.parent: A good answer says that as the scale gets smaller, the map covers more ground but has to leave out small things. A mapmaker chooses what to keep for each scale.

projects.context: In this project you draw five maps, each one covering ten times more ground than the one before. You see what a map keeps and what it throws away as the scale changes.

challenges.title: Directions Without Left or Right: guide a visitor by the compass
challenges.problem: A visitor wants to walk from your gate to the nearest shop. Write directions that use only compass directions, distances and landmarks, with no left or right, and test them with a family member who has never walked there.
constraints: Do not use the words left or right.
Use north, south, east and west, with a distance in steps or metres for each part.
Include at least two landmarks the visitor can see.
Include the name or sign of the shop at the end.
Test the directions on a map, with a grown-up who follows them with a finger.
materials: a map of your neighbourhood, on paper or on a phone
a compass or a phone with a compass
a grown-up to test the directions
general: Walk north for 60 steps to the water tank. Then turn east and walk 100 steps along the wall.
Name a landmark at every turn, such as the neem tree or the red letterbox.
Say which way the shop door faces, so the visitor knows when to stop.
creative: Add a sketch map beside the words, with a north arrow.
Give a second set of directions for the way back.
Write the directions in two languages for a visitor from another state.
challenges.your_turn: Now write your own directions. Test them with a grown-up. Where did they go wrong? Fix your words and test them again. What made the second version better?

flow.do: Read the problem. Look at the map. Mark the gate and the shop. Decide which way the first part of the route goes.
flow.say: Find the gate and the shop on the map. Which way is the shop from the gate? Which direction do you go first?
flow.kid: Find the gate and the shop. Which way do you go?

ask.q: Why can't we say turn left, turn right?
good: It changes when the visitor turns.
The visitor may face another way.
North and south stay the same.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Directions Without Left or Right challenge. You plan a route using only compass directions.

flow.do: Walk or trace the route with a grown-up. Count the steps in each part and note the landmarks. Write your first set of directions.
flow.say: Write the route. Walk 60 steps north. Turn east. Walk 100 steps. Name a landmark at each turn.
flow.kid: Write the route with compass directions and steps.
flow.parent: Check the directions with a compass. If you cannot walk it, use the map with its scale.

flow.do: Give the directions to a grown-up who has not seen them. They follow them on the map with a finger. Note where they go wrong.
flow.say: Read the directions to me. I will follow them on the map. Tell me if I take a wrong turn.
flow.kid: Give the directions to a grown-up. Where do they go wrong?

check.q: A visitor facing east is told to walk forward 50 steps. Another visitor facing north is told the same. Do they end up in the same place?
options: No, they go in different directions
Yes, forward is always the same
Yes, if they walk the same number of steps
check.why: Forward depends on which way you face. The first goes east and the second goes north. North, south, east and west do not change when you turn.

flow.context: In this step you test your directions on a real reader.

flow.do: Fix the parts where the reader went wrong. Make the directions clearer. Test them once more.
flow.say: Where did the reader go wrong? What would make that part clearer?
flow.kid: Fix the unclear parts. Test again.
flow.think: What is the hardest part of giving directions to a stranger?

challenges.context: This is a wayfinding challenge. You write directions that use only compass directions, steps and landmarks, and test them on another person.

setup.art: A map of a neighbourhood with a gate marked and a shop marked, and a dotted line of the route with north arrows and numbers.
setup.caption: 1. Plan the route on the map.

setup.art: A child with a notebook and a compass in her hand pointing along a footpath, counting steps.
setup.caption: 2. Walk the route and count steps.

setup.caption: 3. Test the directions on a reader.

challenges.title: A Map to Touch: make a map that a blindfolded friend can read
challenges.problem: Make a map of a room that a friend wearing a blindfold can read with their fingers, and use it to find a hidden object in the room.
constraints: Use only things that can be felt, such as string, cloth, sand paper, bottle caps and clay.
Show the walls, the door and at least three pieces of furniture.
Use a different texture for each kind of thing, and keep a key made of touch.
Keep the map the same shape as the room, with the same scale for all walls.
Test the map with a friend or a grown-up wearing a blindfold.
materials: string or thick rope for the walls
a piece of sandpaper, a piece of cloth and a piece of foil for different textures
bottle caps or small clay shapes for furniture
general: Use rope for walls, a gap in the rope for the door, and bottle caps for furniture.
Use sandpaper for the carpet and foil for a window.
Put a small knob of clay to mark north.
creative: Use a raised arrow of string for the north arrow.
Add a trail of dots of glue for the route to the hidden object.
Make a second map of the same room with a different scale.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your own touch map. Test it. Which parts were easy to read by touch? Which were confusing? Change one thing and test again.

flow.do: Read the problem. Sit with your eyes closed and feel an object. What do your fingers learn? What can they not learn?
flow.say: Close your eyes and feel a spoon. What do your fingers learn? What can they not learn?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Feel a spoon. What can you learn?

ask.q: What does a map need if you can only feel it?

flow.context: This is the first step of A Map to Touch challenge. You think about how a map can work with fingers instead of eyes.

flow.do: Measure the room by counting tiles or steps. Decide the scale. Glue the walls and door onto the cardboard. Add the furniture with bottle caps and textures.
flow.say: Choose a scale, such as one cap-width for one tile. Glue the walls first. Then add the furniture.
flow.kid: Glue the walls. Add the furniture.
flow.parent: Put the door gap in the right wall. Keep the scale the same for every wall so the shape is right.

flow.do: Blindfold a friend or a grown-up. Hide a small object in the room. Let them read the map and walk to find it, while you guide only their hand on the map.
flow.say: Put the scarf over their eyes. They use only the map to find the hidden object. Only move their hand if they ask.
flow.kid: Blindfold a friend. They find the hidden object by touch.

check.q: Why must the walls of a touch map have the same scale?
options: So the shape of the room stays right
check.why: If one wall is drawn longer than it should be, the shape is wrong and a reader will walk to the wrong place. Touch maps need true distances just as seen maps do.

flow.context: In this step your friend reads the map with their fingers.

flow.do: Talk about what worked. Which textures were easy to tell apart? Which were confusing?
flow.say: What was easy to read by touch? What was confusing? What would you change?
flow.kid: What was easy to feel? What was confusing?
flow.think: What do people who cannot see need from a map, and how are they given it?

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a touch map of a room that a blindfolded friend can read, to see what a map really needs.

items.p: On a map, 1 centimetre stands for 50 metres. A road measures 8 centimetres on the map. How long is the road?
items.why: 8 times 50 is 400. So the road is 400 metres long. If you picked 80 or 800, check where you put the zeros.

items.p: A letter and a number that name one square on a map make a grid ____.
items.why: A grid reference names one square. You read the letter along first, and then the number down.

items.p: A map made from 6 holes in the Hidden Hills box missed a narrow ridge. What is the best reason?
opts: The ridge lay between the holes that were poked
The ridge was not in the box
items.why: A map only knows the land where the stick went down. A ridge narrower than the gaps between holes can slip between them.

items.p: Contour lines that are close together mean that the land is gentle and flat.
items.why: False. Close lines mean the land rises fast, so it is steep. Wide gaps between lines mean a gentle slope.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a short ruler on a map marked in real distances
a line joining places at the same height
a letter and a number naming a square
an object that circles the Earth in space
reasoning about what lies between two measurements
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words are used all through the unit.

items.p: Sort these jobs by what the map must get right.
items: working out how long a walk is
planning where a bed will fit in a room
following a bus route through stops in order
items.a: see items
items.why: To plan a walk or fit a bed you need distances to be true. For a metro or a bus route, the order of stops and the places where lines meet are what count.

items.p: One distance from a tower tells you only that the coin is somewhere on a circle. Explain why a second and a third distance help.
items.a: A second circle crosses the first in two places, so the coin is at one of two spots. A third circle passes through only one of those two spots, so it shows which one the coin is at.
items.why: A strong answer says that each new distance cuts down the number of possible places.

items.p: A phone uses GPS to find where you are. What does the phone do?
opts: It listens to timed signals from satellites and works out its own distance from each
It sends your position to the satellites
It looks at the ground with a camera
items.why: GPS satellites only send signals, and the phone only listens. This is why GPS works with no mobile signal at all.

items.p: Label this contour map of a hill: the top, a steep side, a gentle side and a 100 metre line.
items.a: The smallest ring in the middle is the top. The side where the rings are close together is the steep side. The side where the rings are far apart is the gentle side. A number such as 100 is written on one of the rings.
items.why: Contour lines show height. How close they are shows how steep the land is.
items.art: An unlabelled map of a hill drawn as rings inside rings, packed close on the left and spread wide on the right, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Two circles drawn from two towers cross in ____ places.
items.why: Two circles that cross meet at two points, one on each side of the line joining the towers. A third circle picks one of them.

items.p: Draw the Hidden Hills box from above with 6 holes marked and a narrow ridge hiding between them. Show which holes would miss it.
items.a: A rectangle with six dots in a pattern and a thin ridge drawn in the gap between the dots, not under any of them.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the ridge lying in a gap that no hole reaches.
items.art: A rectangle for the lid of a box, with space for dots.

items.p: Which of these is a public service in a neighbourhood?
items.why: A public service is a place that gives help or supplies to everyone in the area. A post office, a clinic and a school are examples.

items.p: A map can be correct and still leave out most of what is there.
items.why: True. A good map keeps only what the reader needs, and a map that tried to show everything would be impossible to read.

items.p: A map of a whole town has less detail than a map of one street. Explain why.
items.a: The town map covers a much bigger area on the same sheet of paper, so everything is shrunk much more. Small things such as lanes and houses become too tiny to draw, so they are left out.
items.why: A strong answer links the area covered to the shrinking and the loss of detail.

items.p: Put these maps in order, from the one that covers the smallest area to the one that covers the largest.
items: A floor plan of a room
a: A floor plan of a room
items.why: Each map in the list covers more ground. So each is drawn with a smaller scale, and shows less detail.

items.p: On a common school world map, Greenland looks as big as Africa. What is the truth?
opts: Africa is about fourteen times larger
items.why: The map stretches areas near the poles. Africa has about fourteen times the area of Greenland.

items.p: A ship sends a sound pulse down, and the echo comes back after 2 seconds. Sound travels at about 1,500 metres each second in seawater. How deep is the sea?
items.why: In 2 seconds the sound travels 3,000 metres, but that is down and back. The depth is half of it, 1,500 metres.

items.p: A survey of the sea floor has lines of soundings 20 kilometres apart. Could a mountain 5 kilometres wide hide between two lines? Explain.
items.a: Yes. A mountain 5 kilometres wide is much narrower than the 20 kilometre gap, so it could lie wholly between two lines and never be sounded. The map would show a flat plain there.
items.why: A strong answer compares the width of the feature with the gap.

items.p: In the Hidden Hills test, where is the best place to add extra holes?
opts: Where the heights change fast between neighbouring holes
In the middle of the flattest area
items.why: Fast changes in height hint that something is happening nearby. Extra holes there are more likely to find a hidden feature.

items.p: Three people disagree about whether a satellite photograph can replace a map.

views.says: A photograph shows everything. A map is just someone's choices.
I need a map that shows the route and the names, not the roofs of houses.
A good map team uses both. The photograph shows what is there and the map says what it means.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say what another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view with a reason, such as the photograph's detail or the map's choices, and admits a fair point from another view.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A photograph shows more, but a map picks what the reader needs, and many mapmakers use both.

items.p: A phone sends its position to the satellites, and they tell it where it is.
items.why: False. GPS satellites send signals and the phone only listens. The phone works out its own position from the timing.

items.p: A phone needs signals from at least ____ GPS satellites to fix its position and its clock.
items.why: Three give the position, and a fourth lets the phone correct the error of its own clock.

items.p: Sort these maps by their scale.
items: a plan of a village school
a page of an atlas showing all of India
a floor plan of a house
a wall map of the world
items.a: see items
items.why: A large-scale map covers a small area in great detail. A small-scale map covers a large area in little detail.

items.p: On a contour map, the lines are packed close together on the east side of a hill and spread wide on the west side. Which side is steeper?
items.why: Close lines mean the height changes quickly over a short distance, which is a steep slope.

items.p: Explain how contour lines let a flat page show a hill.
items.a: Each line joins places of the same height. Together the lines are like slices of the hill seen from above. How close they are shows how steep the land is, and the numbers say the height.
items.why: A strong answer says that the lines join equal heights and that closeness shows steepness.

items.p: Match each instrument to what it does.
pairs: measures the depth of water with a weight on a rope
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each tool measures one thing that mapmakers need.

items.p: Draw three towers, three circles and the one place where they all meet. Mark where the coin is.
items.a: Three dots for towers, three circles around them, all three circles meeting at a single point where a coin is drawn.
items.why: A strong drawing shows three circles meeting at one point.
items.art: A blank page with three towers marked A, B and C.

items.p: Which number tells you how far north of the equator a place is?
items.why: Latitude is measured in degrees north or south of the equator. Longitude is measured east or west of the line through Greenwich.

items.p: Put these steps in order to show how a phone finds where it is.
items: A satellite sends a signal with the time it was sent
The signal travels at the speed of light
The phone notes the time it arrived
The phone works out the distance from the delay
Distances to several satellites give one place
a: A satellite sends a signal with the time it was sent
The signal travels at the speed of light
The phone notes the time it arrived
The phone works out the distance from the delay
Distances to several satellites give one place
items.why: The delay between sending and arriving, multiplied by the speed of light, gives the distance to each satellite. Several distances meet at one place.

items.p: A road is 6 centimetres long on a map where 1 centimetre stands for 250 metres. How long is the road? Would you walk it or take a bus?
items.a: 6 times 250 is 1,500 metres, which is 1.5 kilometres. A child would take about 20 to 25 minutes to walk it, so many people would walk if the weather is fine, and take a bus if it is hot or they are carrying heavy bags.
items.why: A strong answer works out the distance and gives a sensible reason for the choice.

items.p: A flat map of the whole Earth can keep every shape, every distance and every area correct at the same time.
items.why: False. Gauss proved in 1827 that a curved surface cannot be flattened without stretching or squeezing something.

items.p: Why does a metro map not show true distances between stations?
opts: The traveller needs the order of stations and the places to change trains
Metro trains travel at different speeds
items.why: A metro map keeps the connections and drops the true distances to make it easy to read. It is a map that does not look like the place.

items.p: The map projection that keeps directions true, and was useful to sailors, is called ____.
items.why: Mercator keeps directions true but stretches areas near the poles.

worksheets.title: What a Map Keeps and What It Guesses (challenge)

items.p: A child, a delivery rider and an older person each draw a map of the same street.

views.says: My map shows the sweet shop, the park and the school. Those are the places I go.
My map shows one-way lanes, bumps and where cars park. I need the fastest roads.
My map shows benches, shade and where the road is flat. I walk slowly.

items.ask: Which of these maps is the true one? Say what each one keeps and what it throws away.
items.a: A strong answer says that all three are true for their purposes. Each keeps different features and drops others. A map is made for someone.
items.why: There is no single true map of a street. Each one is correct about what it shows, and a map that tried to show everything would be unreadable.

items.p: The Hidden Hills box and the sea floor are alike in one big way. Say what it is, and name one thing about the sea floor that the box does not have.
items.a: In both, you can only measure along lines or at points and must reason about the gaps. A sea floor map has no lid you can lift to check, so nobody can look at the whole thing at once.
items.why: A strong answer gives the likeness, measure and guess, and one honest difference, such as no lid or much greater size.

items.p: Two soundings 5 centimetres apart show land heights of 2 centimetres and 8 centimetres. What can a mapmaker say about the land between them?
opts: It probably slopes up from 2 to 8, but there could be a hidden hill or hollow
It is certainly a smooth slope
items.why: The two numbers suggest a slope, and that is the most sensible guess. But nothing has been measured between them, so a small feature could be hidden.

items.p: India has its own satellite navigation system, called ____, run by ISRO.
items.why: NavIC covers India and the seas and lands around it.

items.p: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres each second. A GPS clock is wrong by one thousandth of a second. How big would the mistake in distance be? Why does this show that satellites need very exact clocks?
items.a: One thousandth of 300,000 is 300 kilometres. A tiny error in time would put the phone hundreds of kilometres from the right place, so the satellites carry very exact clocks.
items.why: A strong answer works out the error and links it to the speed of light.

items.p: Carl Friedrich Gauss proved something about maps in 1827. What was it?
opts: A curved surface cannot be flattened without stretching or squeezing something
A map must always have north at the top
Three circles always meet at one point
items.why: This is why every flat map of the Earth has to stretch or squeeze something, and why mapmakers choose what to keep right.

items.p: Sort these statements by how sure scientists are.
items: A flat map of the Earth must stretch something
Honeybees carry a map in their heads
Less than a third of the sea floor has been mapped in fine detail
Three distances fix a place on a flat surface
items.a: see items
items.why: The first and last have been proved. The bee map is argued about. How much of the sea floor is mapped depends on what you count as fine detail, and the figures change as new surveys are done.

items.p: Label this picture of GPS: satellite, signal, phone, a circle around a satellite, the place where the circles meet.
items.a: The satellites are at the top, with dotted signals coming down. The phone is on the ground, where three circles meet. Each circle is drawn around one satellite.
items.why: Each satellite gives a distance, which makes a circle. The phone is where the circles meet.
items.art: An unlabelled picture of three satellites above the Earth, dotted signal lines to a phone, circles around the satellites and a dot where they meet.

items.p: A sea survey must find any feature 2 squares wide on a map of 8 by 8 squares. Mark the squares you would sound to be sure of finding one.
items.a: Sound every second square in every second row, for example B2, B4, B6, B8, D2, D4, D6, D8, F2, F4, F6, F8, H2, H4, H6, H8, so that every 2 by 2 block of squares has a sounding in it.
items.why: A strong drawing spaces the soundings so that no feature as wide as the gap can slip between them.
items.art: An empty grid of 8 by 8 squares with letters A to H along the top and numbers 1 to 8 down the side.

items.p: Greenland has an area of about 2 million square kilometres and Africa has about 30 million. About how many times bigger is Africa?
items.why: 30 million divided by 2 million is 15. With more careful figures it is about 14. The Mercator map hides this.

items.p: Some people were kept out of the places where data was collected, yet still made discoveries from the numbers other people collected. How can a person find something new in other people's measurements?
items.a: A person who looks very carefully at many measurements together can see a pattern that no single measurement shows. Drawing the numbers as a picture can show a shape that was always in the data.
items.why: There is no single answer. A strong answer says what the person does with the numbers, such as drawing them and looking for patterns.

items.p: A map that shows the same amount of detail at every scale is possible.
items.why: False. A smaller scale means a bigger area on the same page, so the details must shrink or be left out.

items.p: Match each scale to the real distance that 1 centimetre stands for.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A ratio of 1 to 5,000 means 1 centimetre on the map is 5,000 centimetres, or 50 metres, on the ground. Each ratio ten times larger stands for ten times more distance.

items.p: Which experiment would best test whether a bee has a map in her head?
opts: Carry her to a new place, away from any landmark she knows, and see if she can fly home
Count how many flowers she visits
items.why: A bee with only a memory of routes and landmarks should be lost in a completely new place. A bee with a map might fly home. That is why scientists use displaced bees, and why they still argue about what the result means.

items.p: What would you want to find out about your neighbourhood before drawing a map of it for a visitor from another city?
items.a: I would want to know what the visitor needs, such as the shop, the bus stop or the clinic. I would measure the distances between those places and mark landmarks they can see, such as a tree or a temple.
items.why: Any thoughtful answer is good. A strong one starts from what the reader needs.

quiz.p: On a map, 1 centimetre stands for 100 metres. A route measures 3.5 centimetres. How long is the route?
Which map shows a small area in great detail?
quiz.why: A large-scale map shrinks the world only a little, so it can show a small place with many details. A small-scale map covers a big place and leaves out details.

quiz.p: The temple is in square C4 on a grid. Which way do you read the reference?
opts: Find column C, then go down to row 4
Find row C, then go across to column 4
quiz.why: The letter names the column and the number names the row. Run along to C, then down to 4.

quiz.p: On a grid with north at the top, which square is just north of D5?
quiz.why: North is up, so the row number gets smaller. D4 is north of D5. D6 is south and E5 is east.

quiz.p: A map from a few holes in the Hidden Hills box misses a narrow ridge. What is the best way to find it?
opts: Add more holes where the heights change fast
quiz.why: More measurements, placed where the numbers change fast, are most likely to find a hidden feature. The stick and the colours do not change what is measured.

opts: Working out what lies between two measurements by reasoning
quiz.why: A mapmaker guesses the shape between two soundings using the numbers on either side and what she knows about land.

quiz.p: On a contour map, the lines are very close together at one place. What does this tell you?
quiz.why: Close lines mean the height changes quickly over a short distance, which is a steep slope.

quiz.p: On a contour map, a set of rings inside rings with the smallest ring in the middle shows what?
opts: A hill, with its top in the middle
quiz.why: Each ring joins places of one height. Rings inside rings, rising towards the middle, are the slices of a hill.

quiz.p: You know a coin is 10 centimetres from tower A. What does this tell you?
opts: It is somewhere on a circle around A
It is exactly 10 centimetres east of A
It is on top of A
quiz.why: All the points 10 centimetres from A make a circle. One distance cannot say which point on the circle.

quiz.p: A phone uses GPS. Which is true?
opts: The phone listens to signals from satellites
The phone sends your position to the satellites
The phone looks at the stars
quiz.why: GPS satellites send signals and the phone only listens. It works out its own place from the timing.

quiz.p: Why does a GPS phone need four satellites, not three?
opts: The fourth corrects the error in the phone's own clock
The fourth gives a stronger signal
quiz.why: The phone's clock is cheap and not very exact. A fourth signal lets it correct its clock error, which would otherwise spoil the distances.

quiz.p: A neighbourhood map has a key, a north arrow and a scale. What does the key do?
opts: It explains what each symbol means
It says how far apart places are
quiz.why: The key explains the symbols. The north arrow shows north, and the scale gives distances.

quiz.p: A friend who cannot see needs to find the door of a room. Which map is best?
opts: A map to touch, with ridges and textures
quiz.why: A touch map keeps what fingers can read: ridges for walls, gaps for doors and textures for things. A photograph is made for eyes.

quiz.p: Why does Greenland look so large on many school maps?
opts: The map stretches areas near the poles
Greenland is as big as Africa
quiz.why: A flat map of the round Earth must stretch something, and a common projection stretches the lands near the poles.

quiz.p: Before the 1950s, many scientists pictured the deep sea floor as a flat plain. What changed this picture?
opts: Closer lines of soundings, drawn carefully, showed a mountain chain and a deep valley
quiz.why: Soundings that were close together showed ridges and valleys that wide soundings missed. Careful drawing of the numbers revealed the shape.

open_questions.q: What lies on the parts of the sea floor that have not been mapped in fine detail?
open_questions.why_open: Less than a third of the sea floor has been mapped in fine detail, and each new survey finds ridges, valleys and mountains that nobody knew about.

open_questions.q: Do honeybees carry a map in their heads?
open_questions.why_open: Two groups of researchers read the same kind of experiment in opposite ways. Both agree the bee finds her way well. Nobody has settled how.

open_questions.q: How does a brain keep a map of a place?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found brain cells that fire at certain places and in a grid pattern, but how they add up to the feeling of knowing a room is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Can a map ever be both complete and readable?
open_questions.why_open: A map as detailed as the place would be as large as the place. Mapmakers still argue about how to choose what to keep.

open_questions.q: How can the places that were left off older maps, because nobody asked, be added back?
open_questions.why_open: Maps made by outsiders often left out the names and paths that local people knew. Projects that map with local people are still learning how to do it fairly.

open_questions.q: How do animals that migrate across oceans find a tiny island or a single beach?
open_questions.why_open: Sea turtles and birds use the Sun, stars, smells and the Earth's magnetic field. How they put all of this together into an exact position is not known.

maths.problem: In the Scale Walk, a route measures 7 centimetres on a map where 1 centimetre stands for 50 metres. How far is the route? A child walks about 1 metre each second. About how many minutes will the walk take?
maths.explain: 7 times 50 is 350 metres. At 1 metre each second, 350 metres takes 350 seconds. 350 divided by 60 is a little less than 6, so about 6 minutes.
maths.why_maths: Scale turns a short length on paper into a real distance, and then speed turns the distance into a time you can plan.
maths.context: This is about the Scale Walk, where you turn a measured route on a map into a real distance.

maths.problem: A ship sends a sound pulse down and hears the echo after 4 seconds. Sound travels about 1,500 metres each second in seawater. How deep is the sea?
maths.explain: In 4 seconds the sound travels 4 times 1,500, which is 6,000 metres. That is down and back, so the depth is half, 3,000 metres.
maths.why_maths: Timing an echo is how a ship measures a depth that no rope could reach, and the halving is the step people forget.
maths.context: This is about how a ship measures the depth of the sea with sound.

maths.problem: The lid of the Hidden Hills box is 30 centimetres by 20 centimetres. A map with holes every 5 centimetres needs 5 columns and 4 rows of holes. A map with holes every 2 centimetres needs 15 columns and 10 rows. How many holes is each? How many times more is the second?
maths.answer: 20 holes and 150 holes. The second needs 7 and a half times as many.
maths.explain: 5 times 4 is 20. 15 times 10 is 150. 150 divided by 20 is 7 and a half. A finer map costs far more measurements, which is why mapmakers choose where to add them.
maths.why_maths: Counting the holes shows the price of a finer map, so you can see why mapmakers add measurements only where they are needed.
maths.context: This is about the Hidden Hills box, where a lid with more holes makes a better map.

maths.problem: Chennai is at about 13 degrees north and Delhi at about 28.6 degrees north. One degree of latitude is about 111 kilometres. About how far north of Chennai is Delhi?
maths.explain: 28.6 take away 13 is 15.6 degrees. 15.6 times 111 is about 1,730 kilometres. So Delhi is about 1,700 kilometres north of Chennai.
maths.why_maths: Latitude is a measure you can multiply by the length of a degree to turn numbers on a map into kilometres.
maths.context: This is about latitude, which names how far north a place is.

maths.problem: A GPS satellite is about 20,000 kilometres high. A signal travels at about 300,000 kilometres each second. About how long does a signal take to reach the ground? If the phone's clock were wrong by one thousandth of a second, how big would the error in distance be?
maths.answer: About 0.07 seconds. An error of about 300 kilometres.
maths.explain: 20,000 divided by 300,000 is about 0.07 seconds. One thousandth of 300,000 is 300 kilometres. So a tiny mistake in time is a huge mistake in distance, and this is why satellites carry very exact clocks.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a distance by a speed gives a time, and multiplying back shows how a tiny time error becomes a big distance error.
maths.context: This is about how GPS turns the time of a signal into a distance.

maths.problem: Africa has an area of about 30 million square kilometres. Greenland has about 2 million. About how many times bigger is Africa? Why does a common wall map hide this?
maths.answer: About 15 times bigger. The map stretches areas near the poles.
maths.explain: 30 million divided by 2 million is 15. With more exact figures, it is about 14. A map that keeps directions true has to stretch the lands near the poles, so Greenland looks far bigger than it is.
maths.why_maths: Dividing two areas tells you how much a map has stretched one of them.
maths.context: This is about the way a flat world map stretches Greenland.

maths.problem: On a grid with north at the top, you start at B2. You go 3 squares east and 2 squares south. Which square do you reach? If each square is 100 metres across, how far did you go in squares and metres?
maths.explain: East moves the letter forward by 3, so B becomes E. South moves the number up by 2, so 2 becomes 4. You went 3 plus 2, which is 5 squares, and 5 times 100 is 500 metres.
maths.why_maths: Combining directions with a grid and a scale lets you give a place and a distance at the same time.
maths.context: This is about the Fishing Harbour game, where players move around a grid using directions.

maths.problem: In the Zoom-Out Atlas, page 1 has 1 centimetre for 50 centimetres. Each next page covers ten times more distance. How many metres does 1 centimetre stand for on page 4?
maths.explain: Page 2 is 500 centimetres, which is 5 metres. Page 3 is 50 metres. Page 4 is 500 metres. Each step multiplies by 10.
maths.why_maths: A pattern that multiplies by the same number each time lets you jump ahead to any page without drawing it.
maths.context: This is about the Zoom-Out Atlas, where each page is ten times smaller than the one before.

maths.problem: In the Hidden Hills test, round 1 with 6 holes found 1 of 3 features, round 2 with 20 holes found 2 of 3, and round 3 with 24 holes found all 3. How many holes were added between round 2 and round 3? Which round was best for the number of holes used for each feature found?
maths.answer: 4 holes. Round 1 was best, with 6 holes for 1 feature.
maths.explain: 24 take away 20 is 4. Round 1 used 6 holes for 1 feature. Round 2 used 10 holes for each feature. Round 3 used 8 holes for each feature. But round 1 found only one feature, so the fewest holes did not give the most knowledge.
maths.why_maths: Comparing holes with features found shows that the cheapest map is not always the best map.
maths.context: This is about the made-up results of the Hidden Hills test.

maths.problem: A survey ship sails along parallel lines 2 kilometres apart over a sea patch 20 kilometres long and 10 kilometres wide. There are 5 lines, each 20 kilometres long, and the ship sails 20 kilometres an hour. How long does the survey take? If the lines were 1 kilometre apart, how long would it take?
maths.explain: 5 lines times 20 kilometres is 100 kilometres. 100 divided by 20 is 5 hours. With lines 1 kilometre apart, there are 10 lines, which is 200 kilometres and 10 hours. Half the gap means twice the time, which is why deep-sea maps are slow and costly.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying lines by length shows the cost in time of a finer map, so you can see why a survey ship cannot look everywhere closely.
maths.context: This is about a ship surveying the sea floor in parallel lines.

how_we_found_out.story: Before the 1950s, many scientists pictured the deep sea floor as a flat, empty plain. The only measurements came from ships that sailed in straight lines and timed the echo of sound pulses. Between the lines, nobody knew what lay below. At Columbia University in New York, Marie Tharp, a geologist and mapmaker, was given lines of soundings collected by her colleague Bruce Heezen from ships. Women were not allowed on research ships at that time, so she worked from the numbers on paper. She drew each line as a profile of the sea floor and set the profiles side by side. In 1952 she saw a deep, V-shaped valley running down the middle of a great undersea mountain chain. Heezen at first brushed this aside, calling it 'girl talk', she later recalled. But earthquakes plotted along the same line matched her valley. Their map of the North Atlantic floor was published in 1957.
how_we_found_out.who: Marie Tharp, an American geologist and mapmaker, working with Bruce Heezen at Columbia University
how_we_found_out.when: 1952 for the valley, and 1957 for the first published map
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought the deep sea floor was a flat plain. Tharp drew the soundings carefully and found a mountain chain with a valley down the middle.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Hidden Hills needs a grown-up to build the landscape and make the holes, and the box must be deep enough, about 10 centimetres. The first round is meant to miss the narrow ridge, but a tiny bump between holes may stay hidden even in the last round, and the step says this is a real result. A blunt stick, such as a chopstick, is used, not a skewer. Three Distances works on any large sheet of paper, and the three towers must not be in a straight line, or the circles will give two answers. A drawing compass or a string and pencil both work. The Scale Walk needs a phone map with a scale bar, a ruler and a grown-up, and the map must not be zoomed between measuring the bar and the route. The Contour Hill needs a clear box and clay pressed down firmly. The Fishing Harbour game was checked on paper: the six solo fleets fit on the grid with no overlaps. Facts to verify: Marie Tharp's account of 1952, the Cheeseman and Cheung papers of 2014, the amount of sea floor mapped in fine detail, and the date of the earliest Survey of India baseline near Madras.
